agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 34:0, unnumbered). The Hebrew has 'Abimelech'; the packet's entity tag maps him to Achish, following Rashi, Radak, Meiri and 1 Sam 21:11-16. I keep the written name in the translation and put the identification in the commentary.

STEPBible glosses בְּשַׁנּוֹתוֹ as 'when changed he'; I gloss it 'when he changed', an infinitive construct with a suffix. ṭaʿam is 'taste, discernment, behaviour'. 1 Sam 21:14 uses the same phrase with 'in their eyes', which supports 'behaviour' as the outward act. The literal layer keeps 'taste' so the link with ṭaʿămû in v. 9 stays visible.

history.note: [consider] Consider 'Of David' or 'David's' in the dramatic layer. (PS.34.1: "לְדָוִד בְּשַׁנּוֹתוֹ אֶת־טַעְמוֹ")

agent_notes: I did not read קְדֹשָׁיו as 'saints' in the later Christian sense: the word is 'his holy ones' (the set-apart). Radak links it to the nazirite's holiness; Malbim to the ascetics of the nations. I record both in the commentary without choosing between them.

Reviewer request applied: the commentary no longer claims that kefirim 'reduced to the condition of the poor' shares a root with ʿani of verse 7. It cites Metzudat Zion's gloss of rashu as 'from the language of rash, a poor man' (מלשון רש ועני) and says only that the sense is close to ʿani. The verb is from רוש (BDB, HALOT), a different root from ענה/ענו.

כפירים is read three ways in the packet: literal young lions (Radak, Meiri as a figure for violent men), 'great and rich ones' (Metzudat David), people who devour like lions (Ibn Ezra), and 'deniers' of God (Ibn Ezra's 'some say', a pun on כפר). I keep the literal lions in all layers and mention the figurative readings in the commentary. The Targum's 'sons of lions' plus 'the teaching of the LORD' is an interpretive paraphrase, noted but not followed.

agent_notes: Hebrew numbering counts the superscription as verse 1, so every verse here is one higher than the KJV (34:12 = 34:13). The translations follow the Hebrew verse as it stands.

The verb tza'aku has no stated subject. KJV and ASV supply 'the righteous' from Rashi's reading; Ibn Ezra and Meiri also weigh a reading about the wicked who turn back. I follow Rashi, Radak and Meiri (the righteous of v.16) and put the subject in brackets in the literal layer. BBE rewrites the clause as a noun phrase.

agent_notes: Reviewer request met: the claims that this verse is the psalm's center or that the poem opens with God's nearness are gone. The commentary now says only that qarov, 'near', is new in the psalm and is promised to the shattered. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read 'broken of heart' as the penitent; Radak and Malbim as the afflicted. I kept the plain sense and gave both readings in the commentary.

agent_notes: Acrostic: verses 2-12 open with aleph through lamed in order, with vav skipped: v. 7 opens with zayin, and vav appears only inside v. 6 (וּפְנֵיהֶם). Radak and Meiri both mention it. I cite this in the commentary at v. 7 and v. 6, and this window stops before the later verses.

Reviewer request met: stress is now 'next-to-last syllable (milʿel)', and the Ps 51:19 form is described as milraʿ, a stative. Both claims follow Radak on 34:21 as quoted in the packet. The 'one of them' construction, a feminine 'one' with feminine 'them' for the masculine 'bones', is plain in the Hebrew: ʿatzmot is grammatically feminine.

agent_notes: yeshamu / ye'shamu (root asham) is read three ways: 'be desolate' (KJV, Webster; Radak, Metzudat Zion link it to shamem), 'be held guilty' (the usual root asham), 'be condemned' (ASV). The same verb in v.22 and v.23 deliberately echoes, so I keep one English word, 'held guilty', in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry the sense of guilt and its consequence.

Reviewer request met: the verse is now described as an extra pe line after the tav of v.22, closing the alphabet, with pe already used at v.17 (penei YHWH). The YHWH sentence is removed. The packet vocalizes the verb here ye'sheMu (sheva under both aleph and shin), against ye'ShamU in v.22; Radak notes the difference. I glossed both 'will be held guilty' so the repetition stays visible, and rendered KJV's 'desolate' as a mistranslation of the sense 'guilt' while noting that Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as 'desolation' (shamam).

agent_notes: Reviewer request applied: the last clause is jussive. 'al + yaqtul (yeḥperu) is a negative wish or assurance, so the literal layer reads 'let them not be ashamed' and pos 6 is glossed 'let them be ashamed'; the first two verbs stay perfects (Radak reads them as perfects standing for the future, 'prophetic' use). The five English versions split here: KJV/Webster 'were not ashamed' (past), YLT 'are not ashamed' (present), ASV/BBE 'shall/will not' (future). I follow the jussive form of the Hebrew.

וְנָהָרוּ is ambiguous: STEPBible H5102B (nahar II, 'be radiant') against nahar I 'flow'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take it as light (cf. Job 3:4 נהרה); Radak records the other view (flowing, as in Jer 31:12). I gloss 'and they shone' and mention the flow reading in the commentary and a note. The KJV 'were lightened' is kept out of the layers as ambiguous.
